title: ALS or ALS mimic by neuroborreliosis—A case report
case_prompt:
A 63-year-old man was referred for evaluation of progressive muscle weakness suspected to be a motor neuron disease. He was healthy until February 2018, when he noted weakness in his left proximal arm. One month later he developed widespread fasciculations and muscle wasting including his legs, without frank weakness of the lower extremities. By July 2018, within six months of onset, he had bilateral arm paresis and experienced cramps in his shoulder girdle and hands. In August, he was severely limited in daily activities. He denied sensory symptoms or pain. His medical history was notable only for type II diabetes mellitus (on metformin) and cervical spinal stenosis without myelopathy; he recalled a tick bite in September 2017 without erythema migrans.

On neurologic examination in July 2018, there were mild tongue fasciculations but no bulbar dysfunction. Facial strength and swallowing were normal. In the upper extremities, there was asymmetric proximal and distal weakness (Medical Research Council scale 2–4 of 5, left worse than right) with visible atrophy of the shoulder girdle. Muscle tone was flaccid and fasciculations were present in all four limbs. Deep tendon reflexes were normal in the arms and reduced in the legs; Babinski signs were absent. Sensation and coordination were intact. The revised ALS‐Functional Rating Scale score was 43/47.

Laboratory studies showed a mildly elevated creatine kinase (224 U/L) and stable diabetes control (HbA1c 7.2%). Nerve conduction studies revealed a motor, axonal neuropathy without conduction block and preserved sensory responses. Electromyography of multiple muscles demonstrated both chronic and active denervation changes (fibrillations, positive sharp waves, fasciculations); the tongue was spared. Motor evoked potentials from arms and legs were normal. Brain and spinal MRI were unrevealing except for a slight increase in pyramidal tract signal on proton‐weighted sequences. High‐resolution ultrasound of the median nerve was normal, and ultrasound of multiple muscles showed widespread fasciculations with atrophy and increased echogenicity.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Neuroborreliosis was considered because of an incidental CSF pleocytosis and borrelia antibodies; however, “it is unlikely that neuroborreliosis was the main cause of symptoms in our patient.”  
2. Flail arm syndrome was entertained due to prominent proximal arm weakness; yet “fasciculations of the tongue and paresis of lower extremities developing with time suggest an early stage of ALS.”  
3. Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis was diagnosed because “the El Escorial criteria for probable, laboratory‐supported ALS and Awaji criteria for possible ALS were fulfilled.”
